column4: Moses defines “our Lord” as the one who gives every creature its form and then guides it, joining the section’s owner, fitter, and leader in one sentence.
Within Moses’ answer about the Lord, this ayah makes the earth traversable, sends water down, and brings out diverse plants; it supplies the grown terrain to which 20:54 brings the herd.
“Eat and pasture your livestock” directly stages people, herd, and pasture as the provision of the Lord described in 20:50-53.
God brings the earth’s water and its مَرْعَىٰ out of it, an exact occurrence of the section’s pasture family and its producing act.
The fixing of the mountains is the adjacent act explicitly joined to pasture in the section; 79:33 gathers both into one provision-scene.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ names the landscape as temporary use for humans and livestock, the precise bridge the section makes from pasture to worldly life.
The command that the human being look at his food opens the food-and-fodder scene which the section explicitly invokes.
The abundant pouring of water is the first producing act in the sequence that ends with fruit, fodder, and provision for livestock.
The splitting of the earth supplies the opened ground from which the listed human food and animal forage emerge.
The bringing forth of grain is one particular product of the single provision-making work that culminates in 80:31-32.
Grapes and fresh herbage extend the same produced field whose human and animal beneficiaries are named at the close.
Olives and date palms are further products within the food scene the section asks the reader to hold beside pasture.
Dense gardens complete the cultivated landscape before 80:31 distinguishes fruit and livestock fodder.
فَاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا places human fruit beside animal fodder, exactly the paired detail developed in the section.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ repeats the section’s decisive closing: a provision for a time, shared by people and their animals.
God’s creation of livestock with warmth, benefits, and food identifies the herd and all its uses as the Owner’s provision.
The beauty of livestock when they are brought home and when they are sent out to pasture gives the daily movement of a tended herd.
Rain produces the vegetation “in which you pasture” livestock, directly joining the giver of water, the grown pasture, and the herder’s act.
Worldly life is rain-fed vegetation eaten by people and livestock; just when its people think they control it, God makes it a cut-down field, exposing the true Owner and the pasture’s end.
The worldly-life likeness moves from rain and mingled vegetation to dry fragments scattered by wind, a close expansion of pasture becoming debris.
God sends water, produces varied crops, then they wither, yellow, and become حُطَامًا; the producer encompasses the pasture’s full course and its lesson.
The rain-grown crop that pleases its growers, yellows, and becomes debris is explicitly a likeness for worldly life and its deceptive مَتَاع.
The question “Have you considered what you sow?” makes the human cultivator inspect the act whose true agent is identified in the next ayah.
“Is it you who make it grow, or are We the grower?” states the section’s claim that the apparent pasture-owner is not its ultimate producer.
God could make the crop حُطَامًا, directly pairing divine growth with divine power over its debris-end.
After the crop, water, and fire signs, the command to glorify the name of “your Lord, the Magnificent” returns the produced world to the personally acknowledged Owner.
God sends winds and purifying water ahead of the rain that will revive land and water creatures, presenting the pasture’s provision as directed mercy.
The rain revives dead land and gives drink to livestock and many people, directly naming the herd among the recipients of divine provision.
God drives water to barren land and brings out crops from which livestock and people eat; the whole owner-water-pasture-herd relation appears in one ayah.
Every earth-creature’s provision rests with God, who knows its dwelling and repository; this joins feeding, the animal’s abiding-place, and the far-seeing Owner.
God creates livestock for human beings and says “they are their owners” (مَالِكُونَ), placing derived human herd-ownership inside divine creation.
God subjects the livestock so that some are mounts and some are food, showing who makes the human owner-herd relation possible.
The livestock yield benefits and drinks, and the closing demand for gratitude turns use of the herd toward recognition of its giver.
Sheep graze by night in a cultivated field while David and Solomon judge the damage; the ayah brings livestock, pasture, ownership, and rulers’ care into the same scene.
God gives Solomon understanding of the grazing dispute while granting both rulers judgment and knowledge, embodying the section’s governor-as-shepherd sense.
Moses says he beats down leaves with his staff for his sheep, an explicit first-person glimpse of a shepherd providing forage.
At the well Moses finds shepherds (ٱلرِّعَآءُ) watering while two women restrain their animals, an exact Qur’anic occurrence of the section’s shepherd family.
Moses waters the women’s animals, supplying the protective pastoral act left unresolved in 28:23.
Ṣāliḥ calls the she-camel “Allah’s camel” and commands that she be left to eat in Allah’s earth, joining ownership, protected grazing, and provision.
The she-camel is again identified as God’s sign and left to graze in God’s earth, while harming her is fenced off by warning.
God’s messenger protects “Allah’s she-camel” and her allotted drink, marking the animal, its Owner, and its measured provision.
God produces varied gardens, palms, crops, olives, and pomegranates and regulates their harvest, locating produce and its due under the true cultivator’s command.
Livestock provide loads and bedding, and people are told to eat what God has provided; the herd follows the cultivated provision of 6:141.
Homes and portable tents made from livestock skins serve people when they travel and camp, closely matching the section’s work animals around a people and its dwellings.
“Shall I seek a lord other than Allah when He is the Lord of everything?” is the Qur’anic counterpart to the section’s dictionary formula “the lord of every thing is its owner.”
Abraham names the one who created him as the one who guides him, binding personal Lordship to the guiding act just as the section does.
Abraham immediately names that same Lord as the one who feeds and gives drink, completing the guide-and-provision relation.
Every creature is held by its forelock, while “my Lord is on a straight path”; control of the creature and right direction meet in one declaration of personal Lordship.
“My Lord is guardian over all things” gives the section’s owner the shepherd’s developed function of encompassing and preserving what is under his care.
God makes the stars means by which people are guided through land and sea, bringing the section’s star-watching sense of رعي into contact with guidance.
“By the star they are guided” directly meets the section’s secondary act of watching stars with its image of a guide leading others.
God makes leaders who guide by His command, a human counterpart to the section’s leading animals that go ahead and guide the rest.
God appoints leaders who guide by His command, explicitly turning precedence into guidance of a community.
Livestock and cultivated land appear among the adorned desires called the مَتَاع of worldly life, directly carrying pasture’s temporary use into the nearer life.
The “flower of worldly life” is temporary trial, while “your Lord’s provision is better and more lasting”; plant image, personal Owner, and the lasting comparison converge.
What people receive is the enjoyment and adornment of worldly life, while what is with God is “better and more lasting,” the exact inference the section draws from مَتَاع.
Whatever people receive is the enjoyment of worldly life, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust their Lord.
“What is with you runs out, and what is with Allah remains” states in abstract form what the pasture-to-debris image makes visible.
“The enjoyment of the world is little, and the Hereafter is better” closely restates the section’s semantic path from temporary مَتَاع to the preference challenged in surah 87.
Everything perishes except God’s face, and judgment belongs to Him; the Owner remains beyond the things He brings forth and ends.
Everything upon the earth is passing, supplying the universal side of the pasture’s decay.
The face of “your Lord” remains, setting the lasting personal Owner against the passing creation of 55:26.
The owners of a garden swear to harvest it in the morning, beginning a test of people who mistake control of produce for ultimate ownership.
A visitation from “your Lord” circles the garden while its owners sleep, revealing the higher Owner who already sees the crop’s end.
The garden becomes like a field already reaped, a sudden produce-to-waste reversal governed by the Lord rather than its claimants.
The most balanced owner asks why they did not glorify God, explicitly connecting failed ownership of produce to neglected praise.
The garden owners answer, “Glory be to our Lord,” finally naming the true Owner after their crop has vanished.
The garden-holder enters his garden and claims it will never perish, articulating the false owner’s blindness to where cultivated abundance ends.
His companion says entry into the garden should have elicited “What Allah willed; no power except through Allah,” relocating growth and possession with the true Lord.
The companion says “my Lord” may replace the garden and send a calamity that leaves it bare, seeing precisely the outcome the owner refuses to see.
The garden’s fruit is encompassed and its claimant wrings his hands over what he spent, enacting the end hidden inside apparent ownership.
At the garden’s collapse, true protecting authority belongs to Allah; He is best in reward and outcome, joining ownership, protection, and the end of the affair.
Pharaoh’s people follow his command even though his command is not rightly guided, reversing the section’s leader who conducts those behind him well.
Pharaoh goes before his people and brings them to the Fire as a watering-place, a precise anti-shepherd scene: a ruler leads his herd to the worst destination.
Leaders call others to the Fire rather than to sustaining pasture, reversing both the guide’s destination and the ruler’s duty of care.
People who refuse to hear are said to be like livestock, indeed further astray from the way; the herd is present but guidance has failed.
Those who do not use heart, eyes, or ears are like livestock and more astray, marking the boundary between a guided herd and human heedlessness.
Disbelievers enjoy themselves and eat as livestock eat, but the Fire is their lodging; temporary pasture-like consumption is severed from right guidance and right destination.
At the Hour, prized pregnant she-camels are left untended, a concrete reversal of the protected herd gathered around its people.
The people hamstring the protected camel, and their Lord levels them for it; violation of the Owner’s pasture-boundary destroys the would-be human controllers.
The condemned say they obeyed their chiefs and great ones, who led them astray from the path, exposing leadership that functions as misguidance.
People invent monasticism but do not tend or observe it as it should be tended (فَمَا رَعَوْهَا حَقَّ رِعَايَتِهَا), a moral failure of the same guarding root used for a shepherd’s care.
Hostile speakers twist رَاعِنَا with their tongues; the word-family of attentive care becomes an instrument of insult rather than true regard.
Crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit are grown by the rain of 16:10, broadening the vegetation in which the livestock pasture.
رَاعِنَا uses the section’s رعي family in the interpersonal sense “attend to us”; the command to use انظُرْنَا instead exposes a distinct sense within the shepherd word’s range.
The faithful are رَاعُون over their trusts and covenants, using the pasture-root for guarding what has been placed in one’s care.
The repeated description of believers as رَاعُون over trusts and covenants confirms the shepherd-family’s ethical sense of protective custody.
Joseph’s “he is my rabb; he made my lodging good” admits the contextual reading of a human master, preserving the section’s owner/master sense of رَبّ alongside the theological reading.
Joseph tells the released prisoner to mention him to “your rabb,” where rabb is the royal master; it is a clear non-divine use of the section’s ownership word.
Joseph tells the messenger to return to “your rabb,” again using rabb for the king and making the master sense concrete.
Joseph orders years of sowing and protected storage, a governor’s far-seeing care of provision before its future scarcity.
The hard years consume what was stored, showing the ruler-shepherd’s attention to what the productive years will become.
A later year brings rain and renewed pressing, completing the provision-cycle that Joseph foresaw and administered.
Joseph asks to be placed over the land’s storehouses because he is a knowing guardian, a close instance of the section’s governor who protects those in his charge.
Jacob calls Allah the best guardian, directly supporting the protective function that the section hears within Lordship and shepherding.
The claimant describes one ewe beside another man’s ninety-nine ewes, giving a dispute about flock-ownership before a ruler.
David judges that the many-ewe owner has wronged the one-ewe owner, linking care of a flock’s ownership to the ruler’s just oversight.
God appoints David a vicegerent and commands him to judge people in truth, making explicit the governing duty implicit in the sheep case.
God makes livestock so people may ride some and eat others, another direct statement that the herd and its uses are bestowed.
Livestock carry further benefits and bear people toward needs in their hearts, extending the Owner’s fitting of animals for human use.
Livestock contain a lesson, drink, many benefits, and food for people; the herd itself is presented as sustained provision.
God creates pairs and makes ships and livestock for riding, assigning the herd its fitted human use.
Upon mounting, people are told to remember their Lord’s blessing, turning mastery of the animal back into acknowledgment of the true Owner.
Sacrificial camels are among God’s signs; people arrange, slaughter, eat, and feed from them, while the animal remains explicitly under divine ordinance.
The she-camel is sent as a trial under watch, a protected animal whose treatment reveals whether people accept the higher Owner’s command.
Water is apportioned between the people and the camel, making animal provision measured and guarded.
The she-camel has an allotted drink and the people an allotted drink on a known day, a managed boundary around herd-provision.
The warning not to harm the camel defines the protective limit that the false human controllers later violate.
The command to look at how the camel was created brings the work animal itself before the reader as an object fitted by its Maker.
Good land brings vegetation forth by its Lord’s permission while bad land yields only scant growth, joining رب with the differing fate of pasture-ground.
God sends water and brings forth vegetation, grain, fruit, and gardens, then commands people to look at their fruiting and ripening—the producer and attentive observer of the crop’s course.
God spreads the earth, sets mountains, and grows everything in due balance, pairing terrain with measured vegetation as parts of one ordering work.
Water descends in measure and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; pasture depends on provision that remains fully under its giver’s control.
The measured water produces gardens, abundant fruit, and food, completing the provision-act begun in 23:18.
Blessed water descends and grows gardens and harvested grain, beginning a compact provision sequence.
Tall palms and clustered fruit add the visible produce of the rain-grown landscape.
The growth is “provision for the servants,” and dead land is revived by it, naming the purpose and giver of the produced field.
Pouring water descends from rain clouds, initiating the crop-and-garden sequence.
God brings out grain and plants by that water, stating the productive act at the center of the pasture image.
Dense gardens complete the rain-grown scene and echo the gardens adjoining fruit and fodder in 80:30-31.
The enjoyment of worldly life is declared little beside the Hereafter, clarifying the temporariness carried by مَتَاع in the pasture passages.
God expands and restricts provision, and worldly life is only a small enjoyment beside the Hereafter; giver, measure, and temporary use are joined.
The believer says worldly life is only enjoyment while the Hereafter is the lasting home, an explicit gloss on the section’s movement from مَتَاع to permanence.
Worldly life is only the enjoyment of delusion, supplying the warning latent in a pasture that flourishes and then becomes refuse.
Worldly adornments are set against lasting good deeds that are better with “your Lord,” keeping transient possession and enduring value under the personal Owner.
One who receives the good promise is contrasted with one merely given worldly enjoyment and then brought for judgment, distinguishing lasting provision from temporary use.
The question imagines God allowing people enjoyment for years, testing whether duration changes its temporary status.
When the promised end arrives, their former enjoyment does not avail them, making explicit the endpoint hidden within temporary provision.
After describing people entrusted with authority, the ayah closes “to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs,” fitting the governor-shepherd sense and the watcher of where a matter ends.
One who submits to God and does good has the firm handhold, and the outcome of affairs is God’s; the personal Lord owns both guidance and destination.
The unseen belongs to God, the whole affair returns to Him, and “your Lord” is not unaware, directly supporting the Owner who sees where the matter goes.
Each soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, transferring the section’s “look where the affair will end” from the shepherd’s vigilance to moral foresight.
The question asks whether the one who guides to truth is more worthy of being followed than one who needs guidance, testing the qualification of any leader at the herd’s front.
The prayer to be made a leader for the God-conscious treats precedence as a responsibility to guide others, not mere rank.
Those who disbelieve are driven to Hell in groups, a final herding scene whose destination exposes the cost of refusing guidance.
Those mindful of their Lord are driven in groups to the Garden, supplying the opposite final destination under acknowledged Lordship.
Criminals are driven to Hell thirsty, evoking a herd driven toward water while reversing the expected life-giving destination.
The command to read in the name of “your Lord who created” makes the addressee identify the personal Lord precisely as creator.
“Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him” closely parallels the section’s person naming this Owner as his own Lord.
The people are likened to startled wild asses; the species differs from the dictionary’s wild-cattle herd, but the ayah still supplies a concrete wild-herd scene.
The wild asses flee from a lion; this may illuminate a herd moving in panic rather than behind a guide, though the ayah does not mention a leader or pasture.
Livestock carry people’s heavy loads to lands they could not otherwise reach, giving the section’s work animals around a travelling community a concrete Qur’anic scene.
God makes what is on earth an adornment in order to test human action, placing the flourishing surface under the purpose of its true Owner.
God will turn that adorned surface into barren ground, a direct earth-scale counterpart to pasture becoming refuse.
The garden’s water may sink beyond the claimant’s ability to retrieve it, showing that even the hidden source of his cultivated abundance remains outside his control.
God sends rain and grows splendid gardens whose trees humans could not grow, sharply distinguishing the user of a field from its true producer.
God places livelihoods on earth both for people and for creatures whose provision people do not control, widening the pasture scene beyond the human keeper.
The treasuries of all things belong to God, who sends each down only in known measure; provision and its apportionment are one Owner’s work.
God creates everything and determines it with exact measure, closely matching the section’s creator-fitter who measures and then guides.
Many creatures cannot carry their own provision; God provides for them and for humans, directly identifying the sustaining Owner behind animal life.
God makes earth a settled place, shapes people well, and provides good things before being named “Allah, your Lord,” joining fitter, provider, and personal Owner.
“Your Lord” is the creator of everything and guardian over everything, an explicit union of ownership, production, and protective oversight.
Allah is creator of everything and guardian over everything, giving the section’s shepherd-like protection its universal ground.
God distributes livelihoods in worldly life and raises people in rank so that they serve one another; provision and human governing relations remain allocations of “your Lord.”
Flood-foam and smelting foam vanish while what benefits people remains, a specific reverse-angle on the pasture image’s question of what passes and what abides.
The person who “preferred the worldly life” repeats surah 87’s decisive verb and object immediately after the pasture-and-provision scene of this same surah.
The Fire is the refuge of the one who preferred worldly life, disclosing the destination hidden behind temporary enjoyment.
The opposite person fears standing before “his Lord” and restrains desire, recognizing the personal Owner and looking beyond near enjoyment.
The Garden becomes that person’s refuge, completing the opposite destination to temporary worldly pasture.
The seeker of the Hereafter receives increase in its “harvest,” while the seeker of worldly harvest receives only some of it; cultivation itself becomes the choice between passing and lasting yield.
People love the immediate life, naming the preference toward nearness that the pasture’s temporary مَتَاع helps expose.
They leave the Hereafter, completing the same near-life versus lasting-life choice stated in surah 87.
The human being calls God “my Lord” but misreads expanded provision as personal honor, exposing a false understanding of the Owner’s pasture-gift.
When provision is measured tightly, the same person says “my Lord has humiliated me”; the ayah separates Lordship from the fluctuating amount of temporary provision.
The community is commanded to worship “the Lord of this House,” identifying a particular sustaining authority as its own Lord.
That Lord is the one who feeds against hunger and secures against fear, giving the personal Owner the shepherd’s nourishing and protective functions.
Wrongdoers and their associated companions are gathered together before being directed onward, a collective mustering that prepares the anti-guidance of 37:23.
“Guide them to the path of Hell” deliberately puts guidance language onto the worst destination, an exact reversal of the leader conducting a herd toward sustaining pasture.
People assign invented shares of crops and livestock to God and their partners, corrupting recognition of the single Owner of both pasture and herd.
People falsely declare livestock and crops restricted and impose invented rules over them, acting as owners against the provision-giver’s authority.
The people hamstring the she-camel after the command to let her graze, violating the protective boundary around the Owner’s animal.
After the camel is hamstrung, Ṣāliḥ announces only three more days of enjoyment, tying abuse of the protected herd to the measured end of temporary use.
The people hamstring the allotted she-camel and become regretful, overturning the managed water-and-herd relation of 26:155-56.
They summon their companion and hamstring the camel, breaking the watched trial and apportioned water arrangement of 54:27-28.
The condemned drink like desperately thirsty camels, retaining the herd-and-water scene while replacing sustaining provision with torment.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment, extending the fitted work-animal scene beyond cattle.
God drives rain-bearing winds, revives dead land, and brings forth every fruit, a full production scene under one directing agent.
Water from heaven revives dead earth, giving the general life-giving act behind the pasture scene.
Lifeless earth stirs, swells, and grows beautiful kinds after rain; the ayah sets the field’s life-cycle beside the human life-cycle and resurrection.
People are told to look at the effects of God’s mercy in His revival of dead earth, turning observation of the field’s outcome into recognition of its giver.
Humbled earth quivers and grows after rain, and its reviver is identified as the giver of life, making vegetation a sign of the Owner’s larger power.
God drives clouds to dead land and revives earth after death, joining direction, provision, and the field’s transformation.
God sends water in due measure and revives a dead land, combining measured provision with the produced landscape.
Dead earth is revived and yields grain from which people eat, presenting the field’s food as God’s sign and work.
Adjacent fields and gardens receive the same water yet bear differentiated produce, displaying the producer’s ordering within a single pasture-landscape.
God fixes mountains, disperses creatures, sends rain, and grows noble kinds, gathering terrain, herd-life, and vegetation into one ordering act.
God places stabilizing mountains and apportions the earth’s sustenance, bringing fixed terrain and measured provision together.
Everything is created according to measure, supplying the universal formulation behind the measured guidance and provision in the section’s opening sequence.
Earth-creatures and flying birds are communities like human beings and are ultimately gathered to their Lord; animal collectivity remains within divine oversight and destination.
Livestock themselves contain a lesson and provide pure drink, making the herd an internally fitted provision from its creator.
God creates every creature from water and gives its differing modes of movement, a broad account of the Owner fitting animal kinds.
God makes mates among humans and livestock and multiplies them through those pairs, locating the herd’s increase in divine creation.
The call not to take one another as lords besides God marks the boundary between human authority and the single ultimate Owner.
Taking religious authorities as lords besides God shows how human guidance can be mistaken for ownership that belongs to God.
Joseph asks whether scattered lords are better than God, the One, setting competing masters against the undivided Owner.
Trusts must be returned to their owners and rulers must judge justly, joining custodial care with the governor’s responsibility toward those under authority.
God chooses Saul as king and enlarges him in knowledge and body, making a people’s governing leader an appointment of the higher Owner.
Solomon, ruler over people and creatures, asks “my Lord” to enable gratitude for divine favor, acknowledging an Owner above his own command.
Solomon inspects the birds and notices the hoopoe’s absence, a ruler’s concrete vigilance over creatures in his charge.
The God-conscious are gathered to the Most Merciful as an honored delegation, supplying the acknowledged-Lord counterpart to the thirsty driving of criminals in 19:86.
Every soul arrives with a driver and a witness, making direction and watchfulness accompany the creature all the way to its outcome.
God grants brief enjoyment and then drives the recipients toward punishment, making the limit and destination of مَتَاع explicit.
“Eat and enjoy for a little” states the short duration of bodily provision while attaching an approaching moral outcome to it.
Abraham addresses “our Lord” from a barren valley and asks that people be provided with fruits, joining personal Lordship, settlement, and produced provision.
Abraham asks his Lord to make a settlement secure and provide its people with fruits, giving the owner-ruler the paired tasks of protection and feeding.
People are commanded to travel and look at how deniers ended, a direct Qur’anic formulation of the section’s secondary sense “look where the affair will go.”
Deniers reject what they have not yet encompassed and whose fulfillment has not reached them, then the reader is told to look at the wrongdoers’ end; impatience is corrected by outcome-seeing.
